Phosphate: low and high, mild / moderate / severe

Hospitalist Toolkit · Electrolytes tab · adults · SI units · normal PO4 0.80–1.45 mmol/L (2.5–4.5 mg/dL) · check K, Mg and Ca with it
Decision-support draft, not verified. Written by Claude; doses are typical adult doses. Check against Island Health protocols and pharmacy. Guideline = stated in a guideline; Practice = common practice (no guideline sets this).

Low phosphate (hypophosphatemia)

MildModerateSevere
PO4 (mmol/L)0.65–0.790.32–0.64< 0.32 (< 1 mg/dL), or symptoms
SymptomsUsually noneWeakness, fatigueRespiratory muscle weakness, failure to wean, heart failure, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, confusion, seizures
EatingDiet (skim milk 8 mmol / 250 mL); sodium phosphate solution 4 mmol/mL 4 mL PO BID if refeeding risk or weakSodium phosphate solution 4 mL PO BID (32 mmol/day); diarrhea above 32 Local sheetIV first; PO once eating
IV dose Local sheet15 mmol, only if not eating / refeeding risk15 mmol; 30 mmol (15 × 2) if < 0.5 and ≥ 60 kg30 mmol (15 mmol × 2) if < 0.3 (or < 0.5 and ≥ 60 kg)
IV product Local sheetKPO4 15 mmol (22 mmol K) in 255 mL, peripheral OK, over 4–6 hSame; NaPO4 15 mmol / 125 mL or 30 mmol / 260 mL (peripheral OK) if K high or GFR lowKPO4 15 mmol peripheral × 2, or KPO4 30 mmol / 255 mL central, each over 4–6 h
Repeat labs Local sheetNext morning2 h after the dose if acute; 72 h level more accurate2 h after the dose; repeat levels often unnecessary; daily while replacing

IV phosphate: safety

  • KPO4 15 mmol carries 22 mmol K (30 mmol carries 44): give over 4–6 h Local sheet
  • Central-only bags: KPO4 15 mmol / 125 mL and KPO4 30 mmol / 255 mL Local sheet
  • Use NaPO4 (15 mmol + 20 mmol Na, or 30 mmol + 40 mmol Na) if K ≥ 5.0, or GFR < 30 / dialysis with K ≥ 4.5
  • GFR < 30: 50% dose Local sheet
  • Never in the same line as calcium; caution if Ca is high (precipitation)

Causes of low PO4

  • Shift: refeeding (malnutrition, alcohol, eating disorder), insulin / DKA treatment, respiratory alkalosis (sepsis, withdrawal), hungry bone
  • Low intake / absorption: alcohol, vitamin D deficiency, binders, calcium carbonate, Mg/Al antacids
  • Kidney loss: high PTH, ferric carboxymaltose (IV iron, weeks), Fanconi (tenofovir, ifosfamide, myeloma), foscarnet, acetazolamide, after kidney transplant
  • Refeeding: thiamine 100 mg before feeding, start at 10–20 kcal/kg/day, daily PO4, K, Mg for the first 3–5 days Practice

High phosphate (hyperphosphatemia)

MildModerateSevere
PO4 (mmol/L)1.46–2.02.0–3.0> 3.0, or rising fast, or with symptomatic low Ca (grading used by this tool Practice)
SymptomsNoneMostly from low Ca: cramps, tinglingTetany, seizures, long QT; calcium phosphate deposits; AKI (phosphate nephropathy)
TreatmentStop phosphate intake (enemas, bowel prep, supplements); find the causeKidneys working: IV saline (levels fall in 6–12 h). CKD: binders with mealsAKI / tumour lysis: fluids, rasburicase or allopurinol per oncology, nephrology for dialysis. IV calcium only for symptoms when Ca × PO4 > 4.4
Binders (CKD)Low-phosphate diet (renal dietitian)Calcium carbonate 500–1000 mg elemental TID with meals (not if Ca high), or sevelamer 800 mg TIDSame, plus dialysis adequacy
Repeat labs PracticeNext routine bloods (chronic CKD: weeks)Every 12–24 h with Ca and creatinineTumour lysis: every 6–8 h (PO4, K, Ca, urate, creatinine, LDH)

Causes of high PO4

  • Low excretion: AKI, CKD, hypoparathyroidism
  • Inside load: tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, DKA before insulin
  • Outside load: Fleet / sodium phosphate enema or bowel prep, supplements, vitamin D excess
  • False high: paraprotein (myeloma), high lipids, hemolysis, liposomal amphotericin, heparin in the sample

Good to know

  • Never give a phosphate enema with low eGFR, ileus or dehydration
  • High PO4 + low Ca + high K + high urate in cancer = tumour lysis
  • Ca × PO4 product > 4.4 mmol²/L²: calcification risk
